title: The Air's Nitrogen Must Be Changed

scenes.tts: The air around you is about seventy-eight percent nitrogen. Yet corn farmers in Virginia usually add nitrogen to their fields. Soybeans next door, with healthy root bacteria, can often get by with little or none. So here is the question. Why do farmers still have to give plants nitrogen?

scenes.tts: Why does a plant need nitrogen at all? A protein is a large molecule. It builds cells and does much of their work. Proteins contain nitrogen. D N A carries a living thing's instructions. It contains nitrogen too. So a plant cannot grow new leaves without it.

scenes.tts: Here is the puzzle. The air's nitrogen is a gas. Most living things cannot use nitrogen in that form. Corn can stand in nitrogen-rich air all summer and still run short. Nitrogen gas must first be changed into other forms. Plants can use those forms.

scenes.tts: Bacteria, lightning and factories can change nitrogen gas. Bacteria are tiny living things, each made of one cell. Some kinds live free in the soil. They change nitrogen gas into a usable form. Lightning changes a small amount of it. Factories that make fertilizer change a large amount. Fertilizer is material farmers add to soil to supply nutrients.

scenes.tts: A root nodule is a small bump on a plant's root. Beans, peas, soybeans and peanuts can have them. Bacteria live inside it. They change nitrogen gas into a usable form for the plant. The plant sends sugar to the nodule, where it is turned into food for the bacteria. The bacteria give the plant usable nitrogen. Corn has no root nodules. It depends on usable nitrogen already in the soil.

scenes.tts: Plant roots take up usable nitrogen. Animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals. Decomposers break down dead things and wastes. They return the nitrogen to the soil. Other bacteria change some of it back into nitrogen gas. This movement, from air through living things and back, is the nitrogen cycle. So corn cannot use nitrogen gas. It depends on usable nitrogen in soil.
